abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane junctions (EPJs) house the calcium-signaling machinery that mediates calcium; release from the ER and its reentry into the ER. How these opposing functions are coordinated at EPJs is unknown. Here we show that neuronal EPJs are patch-like membrane contacts partitioned into discrete, adjacent subdomains containing the calcium-release and calcium-reentry machineries. Through a forward genetic screen, we identified the evolutionarily conserved FERM-family proteins FRM-4 and FRM-1 as central organizers of this architecture. FRM-4 and FRM-1 assemble EPJs by bridging the membranes, recruiting calcium-signaling components, and establishing the subdomains. Loss of FRM proteins disrupts both signaling domains and attenuates neuronal calcium responses and plasticity. FRM proteins and calcium-signaling molecules undergo phase separation at EPJs in vivo. Purified FRM proteins phase separate in vitro and suffice to partition calcium channels into their correct subdomains. Thus, phase separation creates molecular and functional subdomains at organelle junctions.
